description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition. Moose are native to the northern hemisphere and absent from South America; no ethnographic source records a moose spirit in Altiplano cosmology. The closest Andean analogue is the deer or vicuña as herd animal, but no named moose spirit exists.
source: No attestation in Aymara ethnography (Métraux, Tschopik, Bouysse-Cassagne)
research_notes: Moose (Alces alces) do not occur in South America. The Aymara of the Bolivian Altiplano herd llama, alpaca, and vicuña; their animal spirits reflect these species. Record appears to be a fabrication borrowing North American moose lore.

description: Not independently attested in Paraguay or Guarani tradition. The Cree are an Algonquian people of subarctic Canada; moose trickster figures (e.g., Wisahkecahk as moose) belong to Cree/Anishinaabe lore, not Paraguay. No moose exist in Paraguay.
source: No attestation in Guarani ethnography (Cadogan, León); Cree moose trickster documented in Brightman, 'Grateful Prey'
research_notes: Cree culture and moose are North American. Paraguay's indigenous peoples are Guarani; their trickster is Japeusá or Kurupi. Record appears to be a cross-continental misattribution.

description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Moose are absent from South America; the Muisca of the Colombian Altiplano had no moose in their cosmology. Their water beings include the Monster of Lake Tota (serpent) and lake-dwelling spirits, but no moose.
source: Muisca mythology (Ocampo López, Simón, Piedrahita); no moose in Andean fauna
research_notes: Muisca territory (Cundinamarca/Boyacá) lies at 2500-3000m elevation; native cervids are white-tailed deer and brocket deer. Record fabricates a North American animal into Muisca lore.

description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Tupi-Guarani tradition. Tupi mythology includes forest giants like Curupira (red-haired dwarf), Caipora, and Mapinguari (giant sloth), but no specific 'Mountain Giant' deity by that name. The generic description suggests a conflation of multiple beings.
source: Tupi-Guarani ethnography (Métraux, Lévi-Strauss, Baldus); no 'Mountain Giant' as distinct named being
research_notes: Tupi forest beings are well-documented: Curupira (feet backwards), Caipora (peccary rider), Mapinguari (giant sloth). No ethnographic source names a 'Mountain Giant' as a distinct entity. Record appears to be a generic invention.

description: Moán is a Colombian forest spirit of the Pacific/Chocó and Amazon regions who protects wildlife and punishes hunters who break taboos. He appears as an old man or animal (tapir, peccary) and tests humans' ethics. Documented in Chocó and Andean-Amazonian folklore as a conservation-enforcing spirit.
source: Colombian folklore (Ocampo López, 'Mitos y leyendas indígenas de Colombia'; ethnographic records from Chocó and Putumayo)
research_notes: Well-attested in Colombian Pacific and Amazonian oral tradition. Functions as ecological guardian; syncretized with Catholic 'protector of animals' motifs. Spelling variants: Moán, Moan.

description: Muki (Muqui) is an Andean mining goblin of Quechua/Aymara tradition in Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia. A dwarf-like being with blonde hair, pale skin, and hypnotic eyes, he dwells in mines, whistles to warn favored miners, and makes pacts for coca or alcohol. Known regionally as chinchiliku, anchanchu, or jusshi.
source: Andean mining folklore (Bonilla 2006; Garayar et al. 2003; Lira, Barrionuevo); Quechua 'muqi' = asphyxia/goblin
research_notes: Consistently documented across Central Andean mining camps from Puno to Cajamarca. Syncretic: pre-Hispanic Ukhu Pacha spirits merged with European mine kobolds. Country field 'Bolivia' is correct but incomplete; also Peru, Ecuador, Colombia.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct entity in Brazilian folklore. The name resembles Afro-Brazilian entities (Exu, Pombagira) but no ethnographic source documents 'Muladi' as a specific demon. Likely a conflation of 'mulata' or a garbled Exu epithet.
source: No attestation in Brazilian folklore collections (Cascudo, 'Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro'; Afro-Brazilian ethnography)
research_notes: Brazilian demonology centers on Exu, Pombagira, Quimbanda spirits. 'Muladi' does not appear in Cascudo, Ramos, or Verger. Record may be a corruption of 'Mulambo' (a Quimbanda term) or pure invention.

description: Not independently attested in Colombia. Mapuche lake monsters (Coi Coi-Vilu, Trentren Vilu, serpent of Lake Lanalhue) belong to Chile and Argentina. The Colombian Monster of Lake Tota is a Muisca serpent, not Mapuche. Country attribution is wrong.
source: Mapuche mythology (Bacigalupo, Guevara); Muisca Monster of Lake Tota (Ocampo López)
research_notes: Mapuche territory is south-central Chile/Argentina, not Colombia. The record conflates Mapuche lake serpents with Colombian geography. Real analogue: Muisca 'Monster of Lake Tota' (giant serpent/fish).

description: Los Ahuiillas (or Ahuillas) are Peruvian Andean road spirits: ghosts of murdered travelers who appear at night near abandoned houses and mountain paths. They warn or terrify passersby, reflecting colonial-era dangers on highland routes. Documented in central/southern Peru oral tradition.
source: Peruvian Andean folklore (Arguedas, 'Mitos, leyendas y cuentos peruanos'; oral tradition collections from Ayacucho, Apurímac)
research_notes: Attested in Quechua-speaking highland Peru. Classed as 'gentiles' (pre-Hispanic dead) or murdered souls. Function as cautionary figures on dangerous roads.

description: Not independently attested as a folkloric goblin. 'Los Chamos' is a famous 1980s Venezuelan boy band; 'chamo' is Venezuelan slang for 'kid/guy.' The goblin description appears to be a folk-etymology invention punning on the slang term. No Venezuelan ethnography records household goblins by this name.
source: Venezuelan pop culture (Los Chamos band, 1981-1991); Venezuelan folklore (Castro, 'Mitología y folklore de Venezuela') lacks 'Los Chamos' as spirit
research_notes: Venezuelan household spirits include duendes, el Silbón, la Sayona. 'Chamos' as goblins is a modern back-formation from slang. Record is a fabrication.

description: Luison (Luisõ) is the seventh and most accursed son of Tau and Kerana in Guarani mythology (Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia). A giant dog or werewolf-like being, he haunts cemeteries and burial grounds. The seventh son of a human family is believed destined to become Luison; Argentine presidents historically served as godfathers to seventh sons to avert the curse.
source: Guarani mythology (Cadogan 1966; Métraux; Olivera 2023 'Bestiario nacional'); Decree 848 (Argentina 1973)
research_notes: Core figure in Guarani 'seven monsters' cycle. Country 'Uruguay' is marginal; primary range is Paraguay, NE Argentina, S Brazil. Syncretized with European werewolf via maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus).

description: Luz Mala ('evil light') is the Argentine/Uruguayan gaucho name for the will-o'-the-wisp (ignis fatuus): a floating corpse-fire seen over rural plains at night, omen of death or buried treasure. The 'gaucha' variant emphasizes its pampas context. Feared by rural travelers; said to mark where the unbaptized or murdered lie.
source: Rioplatense gaucho folklore (Lehmann-Nitsche, 'Folklore argentino'; Borges, 'El libro de los seres imaginarios'; Will-o'-the-wisp global comparative)
research_notes: Well-documented across Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay. 'Luz Mala Gaucha' specifies the pampas/countryside variant. Scientific explanation: phosphine/methane combustion over wetlands.

description: Yacumama (Quechua: 'mother of water') is an enormous Amazonian serpent spirit, mother of all aquatic life, dwelling in rivers and lakes. She sucks in any living thing within 100 paces; Indigenous boatmen blow conch horns to reveal her presence. Documented across the upper Amazon (Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil).
source: Amazonian folklore (Zengiaro & Jaramillo 2025; Wood 1907 'Nuttall Encyclopaedia'); Quechua yaku-mama
research_notes: Pan-Amazonian: known as Yacumama (Quechua regions), Minhocaçu (Tupi), Sachamama (Peru). May reflect anaconda (Eunectes murinus) gigantism in oral tradition.

description: Yacuruna (Quechua: 'water people') are hairy, deformed-footed aquatic beings who inhabit upside-down underwater cities in Amazonian rivers. They abduct humans (especially menstruating women) by transforming into pink river dolphins or handsome men, using aphrodisiacs. Victims gradually transform into Yacuruna. Shamans summon them as familiars for healing knowledge.
source: Amazonian shamanism (Beyer 2009 'Singing to the Plants'; Luna 'Vegetalismo'; Pantone, Tindall 2008)
research_notes: Central to mestizo ayahuasca shamanism (vegetalismo) in Peru/Ecuador. Quechua yaku-runa = water-human. Distinct from Yacumama (serpent mother); Yacuruna are a race of humanoid water spirits.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct water spirit. 'Yaguarón' is a Paraguayan city named from Guarani 'jaguar-ú' (big dog/jaguar). Guarani myth mentions a primordial giant jaguar/dog, but no named water spirit 'Yaguarón' exists. The record conflates toponymy with mythology.
source: Guarani toponymy (Yaguarón city etymology); Guarani mythology (Métraux) mentions celestial jaguar, not water spirit Yaguarón
research_notes: Yaguarón city founded 1539 as Franciscan mission. Guarani 'jaguarete' = jaguar; 'jaguarete-ú' = big jaguar. No ethnographic source describes a water spirit by this name. Closest: Mbói Tu'ĩ (water serpent god) or Yaguareté (jaguar deity).

description: The record describes the Peuchen (Piuchén), not a rabbit. Peuchen is a Mapuche/Chilote vampiric shapeshifter: a winged serpent that drains blood from livestock and humans, whistles to stun prey, and transforms into birds, bats, or humans. Only the machi (shaman) can defeat it. The 'rabbit' label is a complete misattribution.
source: Mapuche/Chilote mythology (Guevara 1908; Vicuña Cifuentes 1915; Pérez 2004; DK 2024); Mapudungun piwichen = 'dry people'
research_notes: Slug 'rabbit-mapuche' is erroneous. The described being is Peuchen (Piuchén, Pihuichén), a major Mapuche/Chilote creature. No 'rabbit shapeshifter' exists in Mapuche lore. Correction: this entry should be 'peuchen-mapuche'.

description: Not independently attested as a named Aymara spirit. Aymara cosmology includes animal spirits (fox, condor, llama) but no specific 'raven animal-spirit' guardian of oceans (ravens are rare/absent on Altiplano; condor fills the raptor role). The description borrows Pacific Northwest raven lore.
source: Aymara ethnography (Bouysse-Cassagne, Tschopik, Métraux); no raven spirit in Altiplano fauna
research_notes: Common raven (Corvus corax) does not inhabit the Bolivian Altiplano; Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) is the cultural raptor. Record appears to project North American raven trickster onto Aymara culture.

description: Not independently attested as a named Tupi entity. Tupi-Guarani mythology includes fox tricksters (e.g., Aguara in Guarani) but no specific 'Fox Nature-Spirit' with the described crystalline, celestial attributes. The elaborate description appears to be a modern literary invention.
source: Tupi-Guarani ethnography (Métraux, Baldus, Lévi-Strauss); Guarani fox trickster Aguara documented
research_notes: Guarani has Aguara (fox trickster) and Aguara-tunpa (fox god), but the 'celestial guardian of Atlantic rainforests with luminescent spores' description has no ethnographic basis. Record is a creative expansion, not folklore.

description: Not independently attested. Duplicate of the Brazil entry with identical fabricated description. Guarani fox figures (Aguara) are tricksters, not celestial guardians with stardust tails. No Paraguayan ethnography supports this specific entity.
source: Guarani mythology (Métraux, Cadogan); no 'Fox Nature-Spirit' as described
research_notes: Duplicate fabrication across Brazil/Paraguay entries. Guarani Aguara is a trickster who steals fire and teaches farming; the 'celestial fox' description is modern fantasy.

description: Not independently attested. Salmon (Salmo salar, Oncorhynchus) are native to the northern hemisphere and absent from Paraguay's subtropical/tropical rivers. Guarani mythology has no salmon deity. The record appears to project Pacific Northwest salmon ceremonies onto South America.
source: Guarani mythology (Métraux, Cadogan); ichthyogeography of Paraguay-Paraná basin (no salmonids)
research_notes: Paraguay's fish fauna: surubí, dorado, pacu, piraña. Salmon never occurred naturally. Guarani water deities: Mbói Tu'ĩ (water serpent), Yaci Yateré (yerba mate). Fabrication.

description: Not independently attested. Duplicate of the Paraguay entry with same biological impossibility. No salmon in any South American indigenous tradition; the genus Oncorhynchus is North Pacific, Salmo is North Atlantic. The 'South America' culture label compounds the error.
source: Ichthyogeography (no native salmonids in South America); Guarani/Tupi/Andean mythology lacks salmon beings
research_notes: Duplicate fabrication. Andean high-altitude lakes have Orestias (killifish) and Trichomycterus (catfish), not salmon. Record is biologically impossible.

description: Not independently attested in Colombia. The Olmecs were a Mesoamerican civilization (Veracruz/Tabasco, Mexico, 1400-400 BCE), not Colombian. Colombia's pre-Hispanic cultures include Muisca, Quimbaya, Tairona, San Agustín. 'Shade' as a ghost type is European; no Olmec ghost tradition exists in Colombia.
source: Mesoamerican archaeology (Olmec heartland = Gulf Coast Mexico); Colombian archaeology (Muisca, Quimbaya, etc.)
research_notes: Geographical/temporal error: Olmecs ≠ Colombia. Colombian 'shade' beings: Muisca have ancestors (mummies), not 'shades.' Record confuses Mesoamerican and Andean zones.

description: Partially attested but gender is incorrect. The Muisca sun deity is Sué (Xué, Zuhé), a male god, not a goddess. Sué was husband of Chía (moon goddess), worshipped at the Sun Temple of Sugamuxi (Sogamoso). The record's 'Sun Goddess' reflects a common modern error reversing the gender.
source: Muisca religion (Ocampo López 2013; Simón, Piedrahita); Sué = male sun god, Chía = female moon goddess
research_notes: Core Muisca deity pair: Sué (sun, male) and Chía (moon, female). Bochica (culture hero) sometimes conflated with Sué. The 'goddess' label is wrong; the being (Sué) is real.

description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Brazilian Cerrado folklore. The name 'Sungrasspan' appears to be an English portmanteau ('sun grass span'). Brazilian savanna spirits include Caipora, Curupira, and local 'encantados,' but no specific 'Sungrasspan' is documented.
source: Brazilian Cerrado folklore (Cascudo, 'Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro'; ethnographies of Goiás/Tocantins); no 'Sungrasspan'
research_notes: Name structure suggests modern English invention. Cerrado guardian spirits are typically Caipora (forest) or region-specific encantados. Record appears fabricated.

description: Supay is the Inca/Quechua/Aymara lord of Uku Pacha (the underworld), an ambivalent deity of death, shadows, and mineral wealth. Originally neutral (allisupa = good spirit, mana allisupa = bad), he was syncretized with the Christian Devil. Ruler of the dead's journey, master of mines, honored by miners as 'El Tío.' Brother of Inti, Illapa, Mama Quilla.
source: Inca/Andean mythology (Taylor 2000; Santo Tomás 1560; González Holguín 1608; Arguedas; Cieza de León; Guamán Poma)
research_notes: Central Andean deity. 'Water spirit' archetype in record is wrong; Supay is chthonic/underworld, not aquatic. Country 'Peru' correct but range includes Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile, Argentina.

description: Saci Pererê is Brazil's most iconic trickster: a one-legged black youth wearing a red magical cap, smoking a pipe, traveling in dust devils (wind swirls). He plays pranks, hides objects, braids horse manes, and can be captured by throwing a sieve into his whirlwind and stealing his cap. Originates from Tupi-Guarani 'Maty-taperé' merged with African (Quimbanda) and European (folklore) elements.
source: Brazilian folklore (Cascudo 'Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro'; 'Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros'; verified living tradition)
research_notes: National symbol of Brazil. Tupi 'saci' = Maty-taperé (forest spirit); African influence: cap/pipe from Quimbanda Exu; European: one-legged dwarf motif. Pan-Brazilian with regional variants (Saci-cererê, Saci-trique).

description: Jarjacha is a cursed screaming beast of the Peruvian Andes (Ayacucho, Apurímac, Huancavelica). A human transformed by divine punishment for grave sins (incest, sacrilege), it roams high peaks at night emitting terrifying screams that portent death. Only spiritual cleansing by a healer can free the cursed soul. Documented in Quechua oral tradition.
source: Peruvian Andean folklore (Arguedas 'Mitos, leyendas y cuentos peruanos'; oral collections from Ayacucho/Apurímac)
research_notes: Quechua 'jarja' = scream/howl + '-cha' = diminutive/pejorative. Functions as moral enforcer: punishes taboo-breakers. Living tradition in southern highlands.

description: Invunche (Imbunche) is a Chilote monster from Chiloé Island, Chile: a kidnapped infant deformed by a brujo (warlock) — leg twisted over back, tongue forked, skin blue, fed on black cat's milk and human flesh. Guards the warlock's cave entrance, acts as advisor and instrument of curses. Created through ritual torture of a firstborn under nine days old.
source: Chilote mythology (Lira 2013; Chiloé Mitológico; Chatwin 'In Patagonia'; Moore 'Swamp Thing'; Allende 'Portrait in Sepia')
research_notes: Core figure in Chilote brujería. Mapudungun ifünche = 'short person.' Distinct from mainland Mapuche beings. Living tradition on Chiloé.

description: Not independently attested. The Ashanti are a West African people (Ghana); elk (Cervus canadensis) are North American/Eurasian. Neither exists in Paraguay. The described being (mudcloth patterns, boubou robes, gris-gris) is explicitly West African, transplanted to Paraguay without basis.
source: Ashanti ethnography (Rattray, 'Ashanti'); Paraguay fauna (no elk); Guarani mythology (no Ashanti beings)
research_notes: Complete geographical/cultural fabrication. Ashanti = Ghana; elk = Holarctic; Paraguay = subtropical South America. Record appears to be a random cross-continental mashup.

description: Not independently attested. The Burmese (Myanmar) and elk (Cervus canadensis) are absent from Chile. Chile's native cervids are huemul (Hippocamelus bisulcus) and pudú (Pudu puda). The described being (longyi, headwrap, bamboo staff, water buffalo drum) is explicitly Burmese, transplanted to Chile without basis.
source: Chilean fauna (huemul, pudú only); Mapuche/Chilote mythology (no Burmese beings); Burmese ethnography
research_notes: Complete fabrication. Burma/Myanmar = Southeast Asia; Chile = southern South America. Mapuche have no elk spirits; huemul is sacred but not an 'elk nature-spirit.'

description: Partially attested but misnamed. Guarani mythology includes the Celestial Jaguar (Jaguarete, Jaguareté) — a primordial jaguar deity associated with the sky, twins, and ancestral souls — but 'panther' (leopard) is an Old World term. No 'Panther Deity' as distinct entity; the Celestial Jaguar fills this role.
source: Guarani mythology (Métraux; Cadogan 1966 'Animal and Plant Cults'); Celestial Jaguar cycle
research_notes: Guarani: jaguarete = jaguar (Panthera onca). 'Panther' is taxonomically wrong (Panthera pardus = leopard, absent from Americas). The Celestial Jaguar is attested; the record's 'Panther Deity' is a terminological error for it.

description: Not independently attested. The Dogon are a West African people (Mali); panthers (leopards) and Dogon cosmology are absent from Chile. The described 'lake-embodying panther spirit' has no basis in Mapuche or Chilote mythology. Complete cross-continental fabrication.
source: Dogon ethnography (Griaule, Dieterlen); Mapuche/Chilote mythology (no Dogon, no panther/leopard beings)
research_notes: Dogon = Mali, West Africa. Chile's felids: puma, guiña, colocolo. No leopards. Mapuche have puma spirits (Ngürü), Chilote have sea spirits (Pincoya, Caleuche). Record is a random mashup.

description: Papa-Figo (Papão) is a Brazilian bogeyman: a liver-eating demon that possesses those who eat pork, especially on Fridays or during Lent. Used to frighten children into obedience. Syncretic: African (Quimbanda) pork taboos merged with European 'bogeyman' and Catholic dietary rules. 'Figo' may derive from 'fig' (slang for liver) or be a corruption of 'Papão.'
source: Brazilian folklore (Cascudo 'Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro'; 'Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros'; oral tradition)
research_notes: Known across Brazil, especially Northeast. Variant names: Papão, Papa-Figo, Pai-do-Mato. Functions as dietary/behavioral enforcement for children. Afro-Catholic syncretism.

description: Patasola ('single leg') is a Colombian vampire forest spirit. She appears as a beautiful woman to lure male hunters deep into the jungle, then reveals her true form: one-legged, one-breasted, fanged, with bovine hoof. She devours flesh and drinks blood. Origin varies: scorned mother, unfaithful wife, or wicked woman mutilated as punishment. Protects forest animals from human predation.
source: Colombian folklore (Ocampo López 2006 'Mitos, Leyendas Y Relatos Colombianos'; Pacific/Chocó oral tradition; Hellman & Hall 2012)
research_notes: Major figure in Colombian Pacific folklore. Related to Tunda (wooden leg), La Sayona (Venezuela), Sihuanaba (Central America). 'Pata' = leg/foot, 'sola' = single/alone.

description: Pincoy is the Chilote sea god of Chiloé Island, Chile: blue-skinned, seal-bodied with human head, son of Millalobo (king of seas) and Huenchula, brother/husband of Pincoya. He herds fish, guides lost sailors, calms or raises storms, and leads drowned souls to the phantom ship Caleuche. Rival to the Caleuche's warlocks.
source: Chilote mythology (Martínez Vilches 1992 'Chiloe Misterioso'; Vidal Miranda; Baker 2015; Millalobo/Pincoya/Caleuche cycle)
research_notes: Core Chilote marine triad: Millalobo (father), Pincoya (daughter/sister), Pincoy (son/brother/husband). Pincoy = male counterpart to Pincoya. Record's 'guardian/forest-spirit' archetype is wrong; he is a sea deity.
